A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same video-world-model policy-evaluation framework, renamed from WPE to WorldGym. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original gridworld experiments, LIBERO policy rollouts, robot-video evaluations, VLM reward validation, and ablations in Sections 3–5 and Appendices B–D.

after.justification: v2 reports original WorldGym rollouts, OOD evaluations, policy-checkpoint comparisons, and inference-time measurements. Table 5 distinguishes its original simulated results from real-world reference results taken from OpenVLA.

M1.justification: The core DiT/Diffusion Forcing world model and Monte Carlo/VLM evaluation pipeline remain. v2 adds clip-level action dropout with classifier-free guidance and changes the reward procedure to support optional 0.5 partial credit. Matching the prediction horizon to policy action chunks refines the existing flexible blockwise inference scheme.

E1.justification: LIBERO and synthetic gridworld evaluations disappear. v2 adds evaluation on 17 held-out Bridge tasks and new scenarios involving edited objects, distractors, visual classification, and altered language instructions. Existing Open-X robot-video coverage and the Bridge dataset-size comparison remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated TinyLlama action-embedding alternative to raw-vector conditioning in v1 Section 3.2 and Figure 3 is removed. v2 expands the robot policies being assessed, but these are evaluation subjects rather than competing policy-evaluation methods. Cosmos, SIMPLER, and WorldEval are discussed without empirical comparisons against WorldGym.

E3.justification: v1's 32-rollout LIBERO evaluations and Gaussian-action-noise protocol are replaced by matched-initial-image evaluations of RT-1-X, Octo, and OpenVLA, using 10 trials per policy per Bridge task. v2 also introduces model-version/checkpoint evaluations, partial-credit scoring, and a 40-frame A100 timing experiment. These are new evaluation designs, not comparable reruns of v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic OOD robustness tests, policy-version and training-checkpoint ranking analyses, and horizon-dependent inference timing. It removes the action-representation study, context/horizon accuracy ablations, human–video-metric agreement analysis, reduced-frame reward-prompt analysis, and detailed simulator failure cases. The Bridge dataset-size ablation is retained in Appendix F.1.

E5.justification: v1 computes LIBERO uncertainty from four groups of eight rollouts. v2 explicitly reports standard errors across task success rates in Appendix E.3 and adds a correlation significance result, p < 0.001, in Figure 4a. The retained RT-1 reward table still reports four-run uncertainty; the PDFs do not establish increased seeded replication.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the LIBERO results with extensive new policy-evaluation results, including correlation r = 0.78 and OpenVLA scores of 67.4% in WorldGym versus 70.6% in the real-world reference trials. Its distractor evaluation reports 39.4% for OpenVLA, and Table 9 reports 93 versus 33 seconds for horizons 1 versus 4. RT-1 reward-validation entries and Bridge dataset-ablation values are retained. These additions do not establish performance gains over v1 under matching conditions.

T1.justification: v1's formal definition of arm-masked semantic MSE in Equation 3 is removed with that evaluation framework. The POMDP formulation and policy-value Equations 1–2 remain essentially unchanged, and neither version provides theoretical proofs. v2's standard-error formula documents statistical reporting rather than new theory.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes feasibility, action-following evaluation metrics, decoding-design studies, and in-/out-of-distribution calibration behavior. v2's abstract, contributions, and conclusion instead emphasize agreement with real-world policy outcomes, rankings across policy versions and training stages, and evaluation of novel visual and language conditions. This substantially changes the main contribution claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning shape-versus-color discrimination, confusion between physical objects and displayed images, and pretraining/backbone explanations for policy generalization. v1's discussion of underestimating in-distribution policies, overestimating noisy policies, and sparse object-interaction training frames disappears. Brief realism qualifications remain, but the detailed world-model limitations analysis is reduced.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents percentile-based action normalization, a 20-frame context, rollout pseudocode, and graded reward prompts. Appendices C–D provide architecture, conditioning, losses, and training details for the video-based and diffusion policies. The core world-model hyperparameter table and project access link remain, while gridworld and segmentation/tracking implementation details are removed.

R1.justification: v2 substantively positions WorldGym against SIMPLER and WorldEval through its support for diverse morphologies and OOD inputs, and contrasts its flexible prediction horizon with Cosmos. It removes the video-generation-metrics related-work discussion and associated citations while adding literature supporting the expanded policy and implementation studies. This changes research positioning beyond citation-format updates.

P1.justification: The title and framework name change, and the abstract, contributions, method narrative, and evaluation narrative are extensively rewritten. World-model construction and validation are combined in Section 3, policy evaluation is reorganized into Section 4, and reward validation and retained ablations move to appendices. The appendix organization and citation style also change substantially.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around interactive policy evaluation and OOD inputs. v2 adds correlation, ranking, training-progress, and distractor plots, numerous OOD illustrations, detailed task tables, and rollout pseudocode, while removing the gridworld, LIBERO, metric-analysis, and simulator-failure displays. Several robot-video panels are retained and relocated, and the document typography and headers change.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrated LIBERO evaluation and real-video fidelity but lacked direct validation of learned robot-policy success estimates against physical trial outcomes. v2 substantially addresses this gap through matching initial images across three policies and 17 Bridge tasks, with detailed comparisons supporting the reported correlation of 0.78 (Figure 4 and Table 5). Removing useful calibration, ablation, and failure analyses weakens diagnostic transparency, and OOD conclusions remain dependent on simulator fidelity. Nevertheless, the direct real-outcome validation substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central purpose.
